title: New Puppy Checklist: Everything You Need Before Day One | Paw & Whisker
heading: New Puppy Checklist: Everything You Need Before Day One
description: The complete new puppy checklist — supplies worth buying, what to skip, and how to set up your home before your puppy arrives.
html:
Free guide · PawAndWhisker · Updated July 2026

Bringing a puppy home without a plan means three emergency store runs in the first week. Here is the checklist we give every new puppy parent — including the things you should not waste money on.

Buy before day one

  • Crate — sized for adult weight with a divider, not a tiny "puppy crate" you'll replace
  • Two bowls — stainless steel, not plastic (plastic scratches harbor bacteria and can cause chin acne)
  • The food the breeder/shelter used — switch brands later, gradually over 7 days
  • Flat collar + ID tag + 6-ft leash — skip retractable leashes for puppies entirely
  • Enzyme cleaner — regular cleaner leaves odor that invites repeat accidents in the same spot
  • Chew variety pack — one rubber, one rope, one soft; you're learning their preference
  • Puppy pen or baby gates — freedom is earned room by room

Skip for now

  • Expensive beds (they chew them) — use washable blankets for months 1–6
  • Puppy shoes, strollers, and outfit sets
  • Bones, antlers, and rawhide — too hard for baby teeth, choking and blockage risk

Set up the house

  1. Pick ONE potty spot outside before the puppy arrives — consistency is 80% of housetraining
  2. Crate goes in the bedroom the first two weeks (they sleep better hearing you breathe)
  3. Tape cables, move plants (many are toxic), and get trash cans behind doors

title: Your Puppy's First 30 Days: A Day-by-Day Survival Plan | Paw & Whisker
heading: Your Puppy's First 30 Days: A Day-by-Day Survival Plan
description: What actually happens in a puppy's first month home — week-by-week expectations, sleep, crying, biting, and the routines that make it easy.
html:
Free guide · PawAndWhisker · Updated July 2026

The first 30 days decide the next 10 years. Here is the honest week-by-week version — including the parts nobody warns you about.

Week 1 — Survival mode (this is normal)

  • Crying at night for 3–5 nights is normal. Crate near your bed, calm voice, no midnight play
  • Potty trips: every 2 hours, plus after every meal, nap, and play session
  • One room only. A puppy with the whole house is a puppy having accidents you don't see

Week 2 — Routine takes hold

  • Fixed times: wake, meals, potty, nap, play. Dogs learn clocks faster than commands
  • Start 2-minute training bursts: name recognition and "sit" — always ending in success
  • Begin gentle handling drills: touch paws, ears, mouth daily (your vet will thank you)

Week 3 — The socialization window

  • Weeks 3–14 of a puppy's life shape their confidence forever. Safe exposure now: car rides, different floor textures, umbrellas, hats, children at a distance, recorded city sounds
  • Not yet: dog parks and unknown dogs (wait for vaccinations — ask your vet)

Week 4 — Testing you

  • Biting peaks. Yelp once, freeze, redirect to a chew. Never games with hands
  • First "teenager moment": they know "sit" and pretend they don't. Stay boring and consistent
  • By day 30: sleeping through the night, mostly potty-trained, knows name + 2 commands. That's an A+

title: Toxic Foods for Puppies: The Fridge List That Saves Lives | Paw & Whisker
heading: Toxic Foods for Puppies: The Fridge List That Saves Lives
description: The complete list of foods toxic to puppies and dogs — what to do in the first 10 minutes if your puppy eats something dangerous.
html:
Free guide · PawAndWhisker · Updated July 2026

Most poisonings happen in the first year — puppies eat first and ask questions never. Print this, put it on the fridge, and make sure everyone in the house knows it.

Dangerous — call the vet immediately

FoodWhy
Grapes & raisinsKidney failure — even 1–2 can harm a small puppy
Chocolate (esp. dark/baking)Theobromine poisoning — seizures, heart issues
Xylitol (sugar-free gum, some peanut butters!)Rapid blood-sugar crash, liver failure
Onions, garlic, chivesDestroys red blood cells — including powders in leftovers
Macadamia nutsWeakness, tremors, overheating
Alcohol & raw yeast doughDough rises in the stomach and produces alcohol
Cooked bonesSplinter — throat and gut perforation

The first 10 minutes

  1. Take away what's left. Note what, how much, when
  2. Call your vet or the ASPCA Animal Poison Control line: (888) 426-4435 (24/7)
  3. Do NOT make your puppy vomit unless a professional tells you to — with some substances it makes it worse

Safe treats instead

Carrot sticks, apple slices (no seeds), plain cooked chicken, blueberries, plain pumpkin. Check every peanut butter label for xylitol before the first lick.
